Table of evidence sources: evals/README, run.mjs, questions, 6 result files, tests, git history, release notes, live one-shot probe.

Mermaid:
question -> isolated FEYNMAN_HOME + workspace -> /lit -> artifacts -> deterministic scorer -> JSONL/MD

What's genuinely good (bullets with evidence).

## 3. Scorecard
Table: dimension | rating | evidence | why it matters.
Dimensions: determinism/isolation, scoring transparency, failure accounting, raw provenance, construct validity, statistical power, coverage, contamination control, meta-evaluation, process adherence, cost accounting, privacy.
Ratings: Strong/Adequate/Weak/Absent.

## 4. Meta-eval: can the scorer be fooled?
Method: 6 synthetic workdirs, rescore with exact command, commit SHA.
Table of results:
case | artifact | done | valid | title | recall | reading
F1 control 100/100/100 -> surface metrics pass without workflow
F2 fake ID 0/-/100 -> recall is string presence
F3 irrelevant real paper 100/100/0 -> validity/title ≠ relevance
F4 1000% claim 100/100/100 -> no claim/number check
F5 wrong bracketed title 100/100/100 -> title check satisfied by claim prose
F6 no provenance no -> process gate works
Interpretation: 4 false-positive modes; scorer is a citation resolver, not a truth checker. This is expected from README, but release prose ("44 citations resolved with matching titles") can be over-read.

## 5. Release-claim audit
Table: claim | source | check | status.
- 4/4 done, 44/44 citations valid/title: recomputed from JSONL (11+11+7+15; all 1.0); consistent, but n=4 and title heuristic.

- dirty=true on 14/22 rows; 0.5.3 runs dirty.
- no eval after Nov 5 /lit prompt change; 110 commits touch eval-relevant paths; 0 evals.
- cost $0 because no cost block.
Status labels: verified/recomputed/unverified.

## 6. Dogfooding notes
- Live one-shot: `feynman --no-session --prompt ...` exit 0, wrote 17-byte artifact, created .plans/.drafts. Command/log path.
- What helped: system prompt integrity rules, shell access, source-first workflow; the audit could inspect the harness's own evaluator, which is rare.
- Frictions: evals/tests not in npm package; no CLI command to run evals; rescore depends on author-local workdirs; version skew (0.5.65 vs 0.5.69); summary table's "all" row is unweighted mean of percentages; installed model differs from eval model (DeepSeek v4.1 Flash vs GPT-5.6 Terra), so can't compare.
- Self-evaluation caveat: the auditor is the harness; no independent human review.

## 7. What would make this eval good
Prioritized list P0/P1/P2, concrete acceptance criteria.
P0: scorer unit tests + CI; persist artifacts; separate completion from quality.
P1: claim-level audit sample; repeats/CIs; coverage; contamination controls.
P2: cost, /deepresearch//audit, public leaderboard? 
Include example test cases.

## 8. General lessons for AI-eval quality
- Determinism vs construct validity tradeoff.
- Meta-evaluate the scorer with adversarial fixtures.
- Report n, repeats, failures, and what the metric does not measure.
- Gate rules in CI or they decay.
- Contamination: canonical-paper recall can test memory.
- Process metrics ≠ outcome metrics.

content.thinking:
Great. Now, let's consider a subtle bug: `gitInfo` excludes `evals` from dirty check, so a run with modified evals still shows clean. That's fine. But `git_dirty` includes all other changes. In the 0.5.3 runs dirty=true means uncommitted prompt/code changes. Important.

Another subtle issue: `scoreCitations` counts distinct IDs, not distinct claims. A report with one citation repeated 50 times has `cites=1`. The release claim "44 citations" means 44 distinct IDs across 4 outputs, not 44 inline citations. That's a significant semantic distinction. Check output artifact? We don't have workdirs. But code clearly dedupes by ID (`Map`). The README says "Distinct arXiv IDs and DOIs" so it's accurate there, but release note says "44 citations resolved" which readers may interpret as inline citations. We can flag: 44 distinct identifiers, not 44 claims. This is a key eval-quality observation. We can verify `extractIds` Map dedupes. Yes line 96-106. Good.

Also title_match denominator is "titled" = resolved IDs with a known title. If a DOI resolves via handle but no Crossref title, excluded. For arXiv, if lookup fails (`undefined`), excluded from both valid and title (since checked excludes undefined; titled requires resolves). So network failures reduce denominator; README says left out. This can inflate percentages. In the 44-run, citations_checked=44, so no exclusions. Fine.

Another subtle issue: `keyRecall` uses `lower.includes(id)` for IDs, so a cited ID anywhere counts, even in a "references consulted but rejected" list. And exact normalized title anywhere, including a "papers not found" section. So recall can be satisfied by mentioning a paper without using it. Our F2 demonstrates title presence with fake ID. Could test a "rejected sources" mention; not necessary.

Another: `findFinal` picks largest `.md` with sidecar. If multiple outputs, largest wins; could pick a long appendix. Minor.

Another: `done` requires provenance sidecar, but provenance content isn't checked at all. Any file named `.provenance.md` passes, including empty. Our F1 sidecar is one line. Demonstrate? We used a synthetic sidecar. Yes: F1's provenance is "# Provenance\n\nSynthetic fixture for scorer probe." and it passes. So `done` is purely filename existence. Strong point. We can mention.

Another: the summary "all" row `valid` is the unweighted mean of per-question valid rates, not total valid/total citations. With 44 citations across 4 questions, mean of rates = 100% here. def tokens(s):

# Feynman eval-scorer probe

Synthetic-artifact meta-evaluation of `evals/run.mjs` from
[Companion-Inc/feynman](https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman) at commit
`11744290758648c2ecd7c0d6389cdca9ae580290` (package 0.5.69, 2026-11-13).

The point is to test the scorer, not the model: each case is a hand-written
`outputs/<slug>.md` plus (sometimes) a provenance sidecar. The scorer is run
with `--rescore`, exactly as the repo documents.

## Reproduce

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman.git /tmp/feynman-src
python3 make_fixtures.py
cd /tmp/feynman-src
node evals/run.mjs --rescore /work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/fixtures.jsonl
```

`--rescore` rewrites the input JSONL in place with score fields and writes
`fixtures.md` next to it. The scored output is committed here as
`fixtures.jsonl` / `fixtures.md`; raw stdout is in `rescore.log`.

## Cases (all use `q01`, test-time compute scaling)

| id | artifact content | expected probe |
|---|---|---|
| `f1-control` | correct claim + correct paper, arXiv URL, exact title | all metrics pass |
| `f2-fake-id` | exact title, fabricated arXiv ID `2408.99999` | `valid` fails, `recall` still passes |
| `f3-irrelevant` | real paper, exact title, unrelated topic | `valid`/`title` pass, `recall` fails |
| `f4-absurd-number` | "improves MATH accuracy by 1000%" + correct citation | all metrics pass |
| `f5-wrong-title` | correct ID, wrong bracketed title, claim text repeats title words | `title` still passes |
| `f6-no-provenance` | correct artifact, no `.provenance.md` sidecar | `done` fails |
| `f7-bare-id` | exact title + bare ID `2408.03314` (no URL/prefix) | `cites` = 0, `recall` = 100% |
| `f8-rejected` | key paper only in a "Rejected sources" list | `recall` = 100% |

## Results

See `fixtures.md` for the generated table and `fixtures.jsonl` for per-case
fields. Summary:

| case | done | cites | valid | title | recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| f1-control | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| f2-fake-id | yes | 1 | 0% | - | 100% |
| f3-irrelevant | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 0% |
| f4-absurd-number | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| f5-wrong-title | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| f6-no-provenance | no | 0 | - | - | 0% |
| f7-bare-id | yes | 0 | - | - | 100% |
| f8-rejected | yes | 1 | 100% | 100% | 100% |

All results are deterministic given the same fixture text and live
arXiv/Crossref responses. Network lookups were available for these runs.

## What this does and does not show

- It shows four false-positive modes in the current metric set: relevance is
  not checked by `valid`/`title`; numeric claims are not checked at all; the
  title heuristic can be satisfied by surrounding prose; and recall is string
  presence, not use. It also shows two extraction/denominator quirks:
  format-sensitive arXiv ID extraction and process-only `done`.
- It does **not** show that any committed model run contains these errors.
  The committed result files do not include the artifacts, so their 44
  citations cannot be inspected from the repo.

# Evaluating the evaluator: a dogfooded case study of the Feynman harness **Date:** 2026-11-14 **Auditor:** Feynman 0.5.65 auditing its own repository and evaluation code **Canonical artifact:** `outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md` ## Bottom line Feynman ships better evaluation infrastructure than most young research-agent projects: isolated homes and workspaces, a deterministic citation scorer with no LLM judge, per-question wall/token accounting, committed result files, and unusually candid release notes about refusals and timeouts. That scaffolding is worth keeping. But the eval is a **citation-hygiene smoke test, not a research-quality benchmark**. Four of its twelve questions have ever been run, only `/lit` has committed results, and the typical run is one pass over four questions with no repeats or uncertainty estimates. Its four headline metrics measure filename existence (`done`), identifier resolvability (`valid`), a 60% title-token overlap heuristic (`title`), and string presence of one or two expected papers (`recall`). None measures whether a cited source supports the claim attached to it. A six-minute synthetic-artifact probe makes the gap concrete. A one-line hand-written report with a correct citation and a one-line provenance file scores **100% on `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`** without running any research workflow. A report claiming a **1000% accuracy improvement** passes the same four metrics. A correct title attached to a fabricated arXiv ID still gets **100% recall**. A key paper listed only under "Rejected sources" also gets **100% recall**. These are not accusations that the committed model runs contain such errors; they show what the metric cannot distinguish. The eval's own rule — run it before and after any prompt, tool, extension, or Pi-version change — has not been followed in the repository since 2026-09-24. In that window, 110 commits touched those surfaces, including a November 5 fix to the `/lit` prompt after a live workflow failure, and **zero commits touched `evals/`**. The rule is well written but not operationalized in CI. **Verdict:** strong harness engineering, thin measurement, decayed operating discipline. The eval is a useful regression smoke test for citation formatting. It is not yet evidence that Feynman produces trustworthy research, and its 100% results should not be read as capability claims. --- ## 1. Scope and method This case study has two objects: 1. **The evaluator:** Feynman's `evals/` directory — its question set, runner, scorer, and committed results. 2. **The harness as an evaluator:** the CLI/workflow contracts that are supposed to make research outputs auditable (artifact-on-disk rules, provenance sidecars, verifier/reviewer stages, telemetry). | Item | Value | Evidence | |---|---|---| | Installed harness | Feynman 0.5.65; Node 24.21.0; Pi 1.5.0; pi-subagents 0.86.0; pi-web-access 0.47.0 | `feynman --version`, `node_modules/*/package.json` | | Source snapshot | `Companion-Inc/feynman@11744290758648c2ecd7c0d6389cdca9ae580290`, package 0.5.69, 2026-11-13 | `git rev-parse HEAD`, `package.json` | | Eval code last changed | commit `e2bcb84`, 2026-09-24 | `git log -- evals` | | Committed eval results | 6 JSONL files, 22 rows, 4 distinct question ids | `evals/results/*.jsonl` | | Models in committed evals | `ferrylane-openai/gpt-5.6-terra`, `ferrylane/claude-opus-5-5`, `ferrylane-openai/claude-sonnet-5` | result metadata | | Model in this session | `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`; telemetry off; alphaXiv not configured | `feynman status` | | Live probe | one-shot `--prompt` run wrote a 17-byte artifact and exited 0 | `experiments/feynman-harness-probe/probe-result.txt` | What I did: 1. Read `evals/README.md`, `evals/run.mjs`, `evals/questions.jsonl`, all committed result files, the workflow prompts, and the verifier/researcher agent prompts. 2. Recomputed the release-note claims from the committed JSONL rather than trusting the summary table. 3. Ran the actual scorer against eight synthetic artifacts with `--rescore`, to test scorer sensitivity rather than model behavior. 4. Counted test/CI coverage and git history for the eval rule. 5. Ran one small live one-shot probe to observe the installed harness's artifact contract. What I did **not** do: rerun `/lit` end-to-end. The committed evals use a gateway and models this session cannot reproduce; the installed model is different; a four-question `/lit` run takes roughly 10–45 minutes per question and millions of tokens. Claims about model behavior below are therefore about the committed rows and the scorer, not a fresh run. **Evidence labels used below:** `observed` = read from code/output; `recomputed` = derived from committed rows; `unverified` = cannot be checked from the repo; `judgment` = my assessment. --- ## 2. What the eval actually is ```mermaid flowchart LR Q["questions.jsonl
12 fixed questions"] --> R["run.mjs"] R -->|"fresh FEYNMAN_HOME
temp workspace
telemetry off"| W["/lit or /deepresearch"] W --> A["outputs/slug.md
+ provenance.md"] A --> S["deterministic scorer"] S --> M["done, cites, valid,
title, recall, wall,
tokens, cost"] M --> O["results/*.jsonl
+ *.md"] ``` The runner gives each question its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, workspace, and `TMPDIR`; it copies a provider `models.json` into the isolated home; it disables telemetry; and it kills the process group on timeout. It records `exit_code`, `timed_out`, wall time, token usage across parent and subagent sessions, git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, and the absolute workdir (`evals/run.mjs:246-249`, `:279`; `evals/README.md:13`). The question set is 12 fixed items (`evals/questions.jsonl`): | Source | Items | Count | |---|---|---| | Feynman's own paper-discovery search benchmark | q01–q06 | 6 | | LitQA2 (`futurehouse/lab-bench`, CC-BY-SA-4.0), verbatim | q07–q09 | 3 | | Hand-authored, outside ML/biology | q10–q12 | 3 | Each question has one or two "key papers" with expected IDs/titles. That means recall is computed against a denominator of 1 or 2 per question, and the whole 12-question set contains only 16 key papers. ### The metrics, precisely | Column | Code behavior | What it measures | What it does not measure | |---|---|---|---| | `done` | A largest `outputs/*.md` exists with a same-named `.provenance.md` (`run.mjs:87-94`) | Two filenames exist | Provenance content, workflow stages, claim quality | | `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs/DOIs extracted by regex (`run.mjs:96-106`) | Count of distinct identifiers in recognized formats | Inline citation instances; bare IDs; claims | | `valid` | Identifier resolves via arXiv API, Crossref, or doi.org (`run.mjs:111-148`) | Identifier exists | Relevance, support, correctness | | `title` | Resolved title shares ≥60% of its word tokens with a line containing the ID, or first-author surname appears (`run.mjs:150-189`) | Title-ish text near the ID | Whether the *bracketed* title is right; whether the claim is right | | `recall` | Key paper ID appears anywhere, or exact normalized title appears anywhere (`run.mjs:195-199`) | String presence | Use, relevance, whether the paper was rejected | | `wall`/`tokens` | Summed over session files | Measured | — | | `cost` | Sum of `usage.cost.total` | Measured only if the provider model entry has a `cost` block | All committed rows show `$0` | ### What is genuinely good These are not consolation prizes; they are the parts a serious eval needs. - **Isolation.** A fresh home and workspace per question means a run cannot read the developer's real `~/.feynman` or another question's artifacts. - **Determinism.** The scorer is a readable ~300-line Node script with no LLM judge. The same artifact text and the same live metadata produce the same score. - **Failure accounting.** `exit_code`, `timed_out`, `completed`, `key_missing`, and error rows are recorded. A timed-out 45-minute run is not silently dropped. - **Raw evidence design.** Each row points to a workdir intended to contain the full workspace, session JSONL, and `feynman.log`, and `--rescore` can re-score without rerunning the model. - **Epistemic hygiene in the docs.** The README says "treat a single run as noisy," tells readers to inspect listed failures rather than only percentages, fixes the question set for comparability, and commits both before/after runs. The release notes disclose model refusals and known issues. - **Privacy.** Eval homes are isolated, telemetry is disabled, and provider keys are read from the environment rather than written into the isolated home. That is a better foundation than a leaderboard with an opaque judge. The problem is what was built on top of it. --- ## 3. Scorecard Ratings are my judgment against the evidence in this report. "Strong" means implemented and checked here; "Adequate" means present with material caveats; "Weak" means present but insufficient for the claim; "Absent" means not implemented. | Dimension | Rating | Evidence | Why it matters | |---|---|---|---| | Isolation and determinism | **Strong** | Fresh home/ws/tmp; telemetry off; no LLM judge; fixed question ids and model rule (`README.md:9,13`; `run.mjs:63-79,165-199`) | Removes the largest sources of accidental variance | | Scoring transparency | **Strong** | Scorer is open code; every metric has a named implementation | Readers can audit what the number means | | Failure accounting | **Adequate** | Timeouts/exit codes/refusals recorded; but `done` conflates process with quality; the catch-all error row loses most fields (`run.mjs:285`) | Prevents silent success, but not silent degradation | | Raw provenance | **Weak** | Metadata is good, but `workdir` is an absolute author-local path; no artifacts are committed; `--rescore` cannot work from a clone (`run.mjs:267-274`; result rows) | A result file is a receipt, not a reproduction | | Construct validity | **Weak** | Metrics cover citation existence/title overlap/key-paper presence; no claim support, synthesis quality, source quality, or research decision | The measured construct is narrower than "research quality" | | Statistical power | **Weak** | 4 questions per run, one run per condition, no repeats or intervals; 4/4 completion has a 95% Wilson interval of roughly [0.51, 1.0] | 100% on n=4 is not a 100% capability claim | | Coverage | **Weak** | 4 of 12 questions ever run; only `/lit` in committed results; `/deepresearch` wired but unused; `/audit`, `/review`, `/replicate`, `/recipe`, `/compare`, `/draft`, `/summarize` unmeasured | Most of the product's research surface is unevaluated | | Contamination control | **Absent** | Questions use canonical papers (test-time compute, speculative decoding, CRISPR base editing, etc.); no no-tool baseline, no post-cutoff set, no perturbation control | Recall can measure memorization as much as retrieval | | Meta-evaluation | **Weak** | No tests reference `evals/`; CI does not run it; no adversarial fixtures or human audit | The scorer's failure modes are unknown until someone probes them | | Process adherence | **Weak** | Rule requires before/after runs for prompt/tool/Pi changes; 110 commits touched those paths since 2026-09-24; 0 commits touched `evals/`; no eval result after that date | A voluntary gate that is not run is not a gate | | Cost and latency | **Adequate** | Wall time and tokens measured; all 22 rows have `cost_usd = 0` because no `cost` block is configured | Token counts are useful; dollar cost is unmeasured | | Privacy and ethics | **Strong** | Isolated homes; telemetry off; keys env-only; content-free telemetry in the product | Research artifacts can be sensitive; this is handled well | | Documentation honesty | **Strong** | README caveats, known issues, refusal disclosures, explicit "single run is noisy" | Readers are warned about the main limitations | **Overall:** the infrastructure is above average; the measurement is below the claims; the operating discipline has decayed. A fair one-line summary is: *good smoke test, not yet a benchmark.* --- ## 4. Meta-eval: can the scorer be fooled? I wrote eight synthetic artifacts for `q01` ("test-time compute scaling for LLM reasoning") and ran the repo's own scorer with `--rescore`. This tests the measurement instrument, not the model. The fixtures, command, and raw output are in `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/`. Command: ```sh git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman.git /tmp/feynman-src python3 experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_fixtures.py cd /tmp/feynman-src node evals/run.mjs --rescore /work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/fixtures.jsonl ``` ### Results | Case | Artifact content | `done` | `valid` | `title` | `recall` | Reading | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | f1-control | Correct claim + correct paper, URL, exact title | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | All four surface metrics pass with no workflow | | f2-fake-id | Exact title, fabricated ID `2408.99999` | yes | 0% | – | 100% | `recall` is title string presence, not resolvability | | f3-irrelevant | Real paper, exact title, unrelated topic | yes | 100% | 100% | 0% | `valid`/`title` do not measure relevance | | f4-absurd-number | "Improves MATH accuracy by 1000%" + correct citation | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | No numeric or claim-support check | | f5-wrong-title | Correct ID, wrong bracketed title, claim text repeats title words | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | Title heuristic satisfied by surrounding prose (8/11 title tokens, 72.7%) | | f6-no-provenance | Correct artifact, no sidecar | no | – | – | 0% | `done` is filename existence; process gate works | | f7-bare-id | Exact title + bare `2408.03314` (no URL/prefix) | yes | – | – | 100% | ID extraction misses bare IDs; recall still sees them | | f8-rejected | Key paper only in a "Rejected sources" list | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | Recall credits presence, not use | Raw scores: `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/fixtures.jsonl`, `fixtures.md`, `rescore.log`. ### What the probe establishes 1. **A synthetic one-paragraph artifact scores 100%.** `f1-control` has one sentence and a one-line provenance file. It passes `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`. The scorer cannot distinguish it from a six-stage `/lit` run. This is expected from an outcome-based eval, but it means a perfect score is compatible with no research process at all. 2. **The title check has a false-positive mode.** `f5-wrong-title` attaches the title "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" to the correct ID for the test-time-compute paper. The line also contains the claim "test-time compute can be scaled more effectively than model parameters." Because the scorer compares the resolved title to the whole line, 8 of 11 title tokens overlap (72.7% ≥ 60%), so `title` passes. The README warns about short-name citations missing; it does not warn about prose satisfying the check. 3. **Recall is presence, not use.** `f2-fake-id` gets 100% recall with a fabricated ID because the exact title is present. `f8-rejected` gets 100% recall because the paper appears in a rejected-sources list. A report could "recall" every key paper while excluding it from the synthesis. 4. **There is no claim-level check.** `f4-absurd-number` claims a 1000% accuracy improvement and cites the correct paper. All four metrics pass. Identifier resolution and title overlap say nothing about whether the cited paper supports the sentence. 5. **`done` is a process gate only.** `f6-no-provenance` fails because the sidecar is missing; `f1-control` passes with a one-line sidecar that contains no real provenance. The metric checks existence, not content. 6. **Extraction is format-sensitive.** `f7-bare-id` is invisible to `cites` (0), but visible to `recall` (100%) because `keyRecall` does a raw substring match on the text. The same paper is simultaneously uncounted and counted. These are not exotic adversarial cases. Wrong-but-resolvable citations, rejected sources, bare IDs, and unsupported numbers are ordinary failure modes in research writing. The eval's own README is honest that it measures citation resolution rather than truth; the risk is that the summary table and release prose invite a stronger reading. --- ## 5. Release-claim audit The most specific public claim is in `RELEASES.md` for v0.5.3 (2026-09-24): > "On the `/lit` eval with GPT-5.6 Terra, 4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles, and each question ran the researcher, verifier, and reviewer in under 11 minutes (0.5.2: 9-14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations)." | Claim | Check | Result | Status | |---|---|---|---| | 4 of 4 questions finished | Read the 0.5.3 Terra JSONL | 4/4 `completed: true` | Recomputed, consistent | | 44 citations | Sum `citations` across q01/q04/q07/q10 | 11 + 11 + 7 + 15 = 44 distinct identifiers | Recomputed, consistent | | All 44 resolved | `citations_checked` = 44; all `citation_validity` = 1 | 44/44 | Recomputed, consistent | | Matching titles | All `title_match` = 1 | 44/44 by the 60% heuristic | Recomputed, but heuristic-dependent | | Under 11 minutes each | `wall_s` = 652, 628, 578, 650 | Max 652 s = 10.87 min | Recomputed, consistent | | 0.5.2 baseline: 9–14 min, 43/43 | Find the 43-citation run | Only `2026-09-24-lit-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.jsonl` has 43 citations; it is labeled `feynman_version: 0.5.0` | **Metadata mismatch / unverified label** | | "44 citations" means 44 claims | Read `extractIds` | Map dedupes by ID; 44 distinct IDs, not 44 inline citation instances | Clarified; release wording is broader than the metric | | 0.5.3 runs are reproducible from a SHA | Read `git_dirty` | All four 0.5.3 rows have `git_dirty: true`; 14/22 rows overall are dirty | **Not reproducible from the recorded SHA alone** | | Cost | Read `usage.cost_usd` | All 22 rows are `$0`; no `cost` block in the example `models.json` | **Unmeasured** | | Search benchmark: 7/9 vs 2/9 seminal papers | Look for the benchmark in the repo | No benchmark file or result artifact; only the release note | **Unverified** | Two further facts matter for reading the claim: - **The eval is not currently a gate.** Since the last eval commit (`e2bcb84`, 2026-09-24), there have been 110 commits touching `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `extensions/`, or `package.json`; 47 of those touch prompts/agents/skills/extensions alone. `git log --since=2026-09-25 -- evals` returns 0 commits. No eval result after 2026-09-24 exists in the repo. Either the eval was not run, or it was run and not committed; both violate the README's rule. - **A concrete missed regression.** Commit `278e9af` (2026-11-05) changed `prompts/lit.md` because a live run improvised `parallel()` and its first workflow call failed. The fix was covered by a prompt-example unit test, not by the research eval. That is exactly the kind of failure the eval's `done` metric is designed to catch, and no post-fix eval result exists. ### What the 0.5.3 numbers do establish They establish that, on one GPT-5.6 Terra run over four questions, in a dirty worktree, four `/lit` artifacts were produced with a provenance file, and every extracted identifier in those four artifacts resolved and had ≥60% title-token overlap on a line. That is a real citation-hygiene result. It is not evidence of claim-level accuracy, synthesis quality, or generalization to the other eight questions, other workflows, or other models. ### Statistical context Treating the 44 identifiers as independent (optimistic, because they cluster within four reports), a 95% Wilson interval for 44/44 is roughly [0.92, 1.00]. Treating the four questions as the unit, 4/4 completion has a Wilson interval of roughly [0.51, 1.00]. The true uncertainty is wider than either because there is one run per condition and no repeated sampling. "100%" in the table is a point estimate, not a ceiling. --- ## 6. Dogfooding notes I ran this audit from inside a Feynman session and also exercised the installed CLI as a subprocess. **Live one-shot probe.** In an empty workspace: ```sh FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=off feynman --no-session --prompt \ "Create the file outputs/probe-artifact.md with exactly one line: FEYNMAN_PROBE_OK. Use the write tool, then reply DONE." ``` Result: exit 0, stdout `DONE`, artifact `FEYNMAN_PROBE_OK` (17 bytes), and the harness created `outputs/`, `outputs/.plans/`, `outputs/.drafts/`, `notes/`, and `papers/`. Log: `experiments/feynman-harness-probe/probe.log`; result summary: `probe-result.txt`. This is a small positive data point: the one-shot path exits, writes the requested artifact, and scaffolds the expected workspace. **What helped the audit.** - The system prompt's evidence/integrity rules are unusually explicit: separate observation from inference, label blocked/unverified work, verify artifacts on disk, never invent results. Those rules directly shaped this report. - Shell access plus a source-first workflow made it possible to audit the evaluator's code, not just its marketing. Many agent products make this impossible because only a hosted API is exposed. - The harness's own conventions (slugged artifacts, provenance sidecars, raw logs) are good habits for any eval. **Frictions observed.** - **The eval is not shipped.** `evals/` and `tests/` are absent from the npm package (`package.json` `files`; README line 5). An installed user cannot run the harness's own eval without cloning the repo. That is a transparency cost. - **There is no `feynman eval` command.** Running the eval means building the repo, supplying a `models.json`, exporting a provider key, and choosing ids/workflow manually. That is developer-only, which helps explain why the rule decays. - **`--rescore` depends on author-local state.** Every committed row stores an absolute `workdir` (`/Users/advaitpaliwal/.cache/...` or `/var/folders/...`). The artifacts are not committed. A fresh clone cannot rescore any published result. - **Version and model skew.** The installed harness is 0.5.65; the source snapshot is 0.5.69. The committed evals use GPT-5.6 Terra / Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Sonnet 5; this session runs DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. I can audit the scorer and the claims, but not reproduce the model behavior. - **The summary row hides denominators.** `table()` takes the unweighted mean of per-question percentages, excluding nulls (`run.mjs:251-259`). A run with 3/4 completion can show `valid 100%` because the failed question is null and dropped, while `recall` includes the failure as 0. The columns have different denominators. That is visible if you read carefully, but the "all" row encourages a single number. - **Self-evaluation bias.** I am the harness. There is no independent human rater in this loop. The quantitative claims here trace to files and commands; the ratings are judgments and should be treated as such. --- ## 7. What would make this eval good Prioritized, with acceptance criteria. The first three are cheap relative to another four-question model run. ### P0 — make the scorer trustworthy and the results reproducible 1. **Add `evals/scorer.test.mjs` with adversarial fixtures.** Encode the eight cases above. Assert current behavior explicitly, including known false positives, so a future scorer change cannot silently change their meaning. Add a `claim_support` column and make `f4-absurd-number` fail it. - *Acceptance:* `npm test` runs the scorer tests; CI fails if `f2` validity is not 0, `f3` recall is not 0, `f6` done is not false, or `f4` passes a claim-support check. 2. **Persist enough artifacts to rescore from a clone.** Commit a small tarball per run (final `.md`, provenance, extracted citation list) or make `workdir` a content-addressed relative path and publish the bundle. Do not commit 100 MB session logs by default; commit the scored artifact and a manifest. - *Acceptance:* `node evals/run.mjs --rescore evals/results/.jsonl` works in a fresh clone with no author-local paths. 3. **Separate process compliance from output quality.** Replace the single `done` with `artifact_present`, `provenance_present`, `verifier_ran`, `reviewer_ran`, and `quality_metrics`. Derive the stage flags from the session JSONL (subagent roles/calls), not filenames. - *Acceptance:* a run that skips the verifier/reviewer cannot score the same as one that runs them. ### P1 — make the measurement valid and powered 4. **Add a claim-level audit sample.** For each run, sample 20 numeric or causal claims and check whether the cited source contains the number/claim. Report claim precision with a denominator and a human-readable list of failures. This is the only way to catch the `f4` class. - *Acceptance:* a run with a fabricated 1000% number has a non-zero failure list. 5. **Run repeats and report uncertainty.** Two or three seeds per condition, or at least two independent runs for a prompt change. Report mean/range and n. Use all 12 questions when the budget allows; otherwise state the selected ids as a fixed panel and do not generalize. - *Acceptance:* no "100%" claim appears without n and an interval or range. 6. **Enforce the rule or narrow it.** If the rule stays, add a PR checklist/CI check: changes to `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `extensions/`, or the Pi pin must include a new eval result file or a written `no-eval` justification. If full evals are too expensive for every change, define a cheap gate (one question, scorer tests) plus a release gate (four questions, two seeds). - *Acceptance:* the repository can show, for each prompt change, either a result file or an explicit waiver. Today it can show neither. 7. **Add contamination controls.** Include 3–5 post-cutoff questions; run a no-tools baseline; and run a "titles only" control to estimate how much recall comes from memorization. Keep the canonical questions for comparability, but do not treat them as retrieval evidence by themselves. ### P2 — extend coverage and accounting 8. **Measure cost.** Add a `cost` block to the example `models.json`; report dollars per completed question and per valid citation. The current `$0.00` is a missing value, not a cheap run. 9. **Cover the other workflows.** `/deepresearch` is already supported by the runner but has no committed result. Add at least one `/audit` case with a known paper–code discrepancy (the README already names SciCoQA's 92 discrepancies) and one `/review` case with a known flawed draft. 10. **Meta-metrics.** Report citation precision/recall against a human-labeled sample, inter-rater agreement for any human judgments, and the false-positive rate of the verifier. A benchmark of the benchmark. --- ## 8. General lessons for AI-eval quality 1. **Deterministic scorers buy reproducibility at the cost of construct validity.** That is a reasonable trade for a smoke test. The mistake is letting the metric's name do more work than its implementation. 2. **Meta-evaluate the scorer before trusting the score.** Eight hand-written fixtures took minutes and found four false-positive modes. A scorer without adversarial fixtures is an untested measuring instrument. 3. **A rule that is not in CI decays.** The eval README's rule is well written and was followed for two days. Then 110 eval-relevant commits passed without an eval commit. Voluntary gates lose to release pressure. 4. **`done` is a process metric, not a quality metric.** Filename existence and provenance presence are useful checks; they are not evidence of research quality. # Evaluating the evaluator: a dogfooded case study of the Feynman harness **Date:** 2026-11-14 **Auditor:** Feynman 0.5.65 auditing its own repository and evaluation code **Canonical artifact:** `outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md` ## Bottom line Feynman ships a genuinely useful evaluation scaffold: isolated homes and workspaces, a deterministic citation scorer with no LLM judge, per-question wall/token accounting, committed result files, and unusually candid release notes about refusals and timeouts. That scaffolding is worth keeping. But the eval is a **citation-hygiene smoke test, not a research-quality benchmark**. Committed results cover only four of its twelve questions, only `/lit` has results, and the typical run is one pass over four questions with no repeats or uncertainty estimates. Its four headline metrics measure filename existence (`done`), identifier resolvability (`valid`), a 60% title-token overlap heuristic (`title`), and string presence of one or two expected papers (`recall`). None measures whether a cited source supports the claim attached to it. A short synthetic-artifact probe makes the gap concrete. A one-sentence hand-written report with a correct citation and a minimal provenance file scores **100% on `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`** without running any research workflow. A report claiming a **1000% accuracy improvement** passes the same four metrics. A correct title attached to a fabricated arXiv ID still gets **100% recall**. A key paper listed only under "Rejected sources" also gets **100% recall**. These are not accusations that the committed model runs contain such errors; they show what the metric cannot distinguish. The eval's own rule — run it before and after any prompt, tool, extension, or Pi-version change — has not been followed in the repository since 2026-09-24. In that window, 110 commits touched those surfaces, including a November 5 fix to the `/lit` prompt after a live workflow failure, and **zero commits touched `evals/`**. The rule is well written but not operationalized in CI. **Verdict:** strong harness engineering, thin measurement, decayed operating discipline. The eval is a useful regression smoke test for citation formatting. It is not yet evidence that Feynman produces trustworthy research, and its 100% results should not be read as capability claims. --- ## 1. Scope and method This case study has two objects: 1. **The evaluator:** Feynman's `evals/` directory — its question set, runner, scorer, and committed results. 2. **The harness as an evaluator:** the CLI/workflow contracts that are supposed to make research outputs auditable (artifact-on-disk rules, provenance sidecars, verifier/reviewer stages, telemetry). | Item | Value | Evidence | |---|---|---| | Installed harness | Feynman 0.5.65; Node 24.21.0; Pi 1.5.0; pi-subagents 0.86.0; pi-web-access 0.47.0 | `feynman --version`, `node_modules/*/package.json` | | Source snapshot | `Companion-Inc/feynman@11744290758648c2ecd7c0d6389cdca9ae580290`, package 0.5.69, 2026-11-13 | `git rev-parse HEAD`, `package.json` | | Eval code last changed | commit `e2bcb84`, 2026-09-24 | `git log -- evals` | | Committed eval results | 6 JSONL files, 22 rows, 4 distinct question ids | `evals/results/*.jsonl` | | Models in committed evals | `ferrylane-openai/gpt-5.6-terra`, `ferrylane/claude-opus-5-5`, `ferrylane-openai/claude-sonnet-5` | result metadata | | Model in this session | `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`; telemetry off; alphaXiv not configured | `feynman status` | | Live probe | one-shot `--prompt` run wrote a 17-byte artifact and exited 0 | `experiments/feynman-harness-probe/probe-result.txt` | What I did: 1. Read `evals/README.md`, `evals/run.mjs`, `evals/questions.jsonl`, all committed result files, the workflow prompts, and the verifier/researcher agent prompts. 2. Recomputed the release-note claims from the committed JSONL rather than trusting the summary table. 3. Ran the actual scorer against eight synthetic artifacts with `--rescore`, to test scorer sensitivity rather than model behavior. 4. Counted test/CI coverage and git history for the eval rule. 5. Ran one small live one-shot probe to observe the installed harness's artifact contract. What I did **not** do: rerun `/lit` end-to-end. The committed evals use a gateway and models this session cannot reproduce; the installed model is different; a four-question `/lit` run takes roughly 10–45 minutes per question and millions of tokens. Claims about model behavior below are therefore about the committed rows and the scorer, not a fresh run. **Evidence labels used below:** `observed` = read from code/output; `recomputed` = derived from committed rows; `unverified` = cannot be checked from the repo; `judgment` = my assessment. --- ## 2. What the eval actually is ```mermaid flowchart LR Q["questions.jsonl
12 fixed questions"] --> R["run.mjs"] R -->|"fresh FEYNMAN_HOME
temp workspace
telemetry off"| W["/lit or /deepresearch"] W --> A["outputs/slug.md
+ provenance.md"] A --> S["deterministic scorer"] S --> M["done, cites, valid,
title, recall, wall,
tokens, cost"] M --> O["results/*.jsonl
+ *.md"] ``` The runner gives each question its own `FEYNMAN_HOME`, workspace, and `TMPDIR`; it copies a provider `models.json` into the isolated home; it disables telemetry; and it kills the process group on timeout. It records `exit_code`, `timed_out`, wall time, token usage across parent and subagent sessions, git SHA, dirty flag, Feynman version, and the absolute workdir (`evals/run.mjs:246-249`, `:279`; `evals/README.md:13`). The question set is 12 fixed items (`evals/questions.jsonl`): | Source | Items | Count | |---|---|---| | Feynman's own paper-discovery search benchmark | q01–q06 | 6 | | LitQA2 (`futurehouse/lab-bench`, CC-BY-SA-4.0), verbatim | q07–q09 | 3 | | Hand-authored, outside ML/biology | q10–q12 | 3 | Each question has one or two "key papers" with expected IDs/titles. That means recall is computed against a denominator of 1 or 2 per question, and the whole 12-question set contains only 18 key papers. ### The metrics, precisely | Column | Code behavior | What it measures | What it does not measure | |---|---|---|---| | `done` | A largest `outputs/*.md` exists with a same-named `.provenance.md` (`run.mjs:87-94`) | Two filenames exist | Provenance content, workflow stages, claim quality | | `cites` | Distinct arXiv IDs/DOIs extracted by regex (`run.mjs:96-106`) | Count of distinct identifiers in recognized formats | Inline citation instances; bare IDs; claims | | `valid` | Identifier resolves via arXiv API, Crossref, or doi.org (`run.mjs:111-148`) | Identifier exists | Relevance, support, correctness | | `title` | Resolved title shares ≥60% of its word tokens with a line containing the ID, or first-author surname appears (`run.mjs:150-189`) | Title-ish text near the ID | Whether the *bracketed* title is right; whether the claim is right | | `recall` | Key paper ID appears anywhere, or exact normalized title appears anywhere (`run.mjs:195-199`) | String presence | Use, relevance, whether the paper was rejected | | `wall`/`tokens` | Summed over session files | Measured | — | | `cost` | Sum of `usage.cost.total` | Measured only if the provider model entry has a `cost` block | All committed rows show `$0` | ### What is genuinely good These are not consolation prizes; they are the parts a serious eval needs. - **Isolation.** A fresh home and workspace per question means a run cannot read the developer's real `~/.feynman` or another question's artifacts. - **Determinism.** The scorer is a readable ~300-line Node script with no LLM judge. The same artifact text and the same live metadata produce the same score. - **Failure accounting.** `exit_code`, `timed_out`, `completed`, `key_missing`, and error rows are recorded. A timed-out 45-minute run is not silently dropped. - **Raw evidence design.** Each row points to a workdir intended to contain the full workspace, session JSONL, and `feynman.log`, and `--rescore` can re-score without rerunning the model. - **Epistemic hygiene in the docs.** The README says "treat a single run as noisy," tells readers to inspect listed failures rather than only percentages, fixes the question set for comparability, and commits both before/after runs. The release notes disclose model refusals and known issues. - **Privacy.** Eval homes are isolated, telemetry is disabled, and provider keys are read from the environment rather than written into the isolated home. That is a better foundation than a leaderboard with an opaque judge. The problem is what was built on top of it. --- ## 3. Scorecard Ratings are my judgment against the evidence in this report. "Strong" means implemented and checked here; "Adequate" means present with material caveats; "Weak" means present but insufficient for the claim; "Absent" means not implemented. | Dimension | Rating | Evidence | Why it matters | |---|---|---|---| | Isolation and determinism | **Strong** | Fresh home/ws/tmp; telemetry off; no LLM judge; fixed question ids and model rule (`README.md:9,13`; `run.mjs:63-79,165-199`) | Removes the largest sources of accidental variance | | Scoring transparency | **Strong** | Scorer is open code; every metric has a named implementation | Readers can audit what the number means | | Failure accounting | **Adequate** | Timeouts/exit codes/refusals recorded; but `done` conflates process with quality; the catch-all error row loses most fields (`run.mjs:285`) | Prevents silent success, but not silent degradation | | Raw provenance | **Weak** | Metadata is good, but `workdir` is an absolute author-local path; no artifacts are committed; `--rescore` cannot work from a clone (`run.mjs:267-274`; result rows) | A result file is a receipt, not a reproduction | | Construct validity | **Weak** | Metrics cover citation existence/title overlap/key-paper presence; no claim support, synthesis quality, source quality, or research decision | The measured construct is narrower than "research quality" | | Statistical power | **Weak** | 4 questions per run, one run per condition, no repeats or intervals; 4/4 completion has a 95% Wilson interval of roughly [0.51, 1.0] | 100% on n=4 is not a 100% capability claim | | Coverage | **Weak** | 4 of 12 questions have committed results; only `/lit` in committed results; `/deepresearch` wired but unused; `/audit`, `/review`, `/replicate`, `/recipe`, `/compare`, `/draft`, `/summarize` unmeasured | Most of the product's research surface is unevaluated | | Contamination control | **Absent** | Questions use canonical papers (test-time compute, speculative decoding, CRISPR base editing, etc.); no no-tool baseline, no post-cutoff set, no perturbation control | Recall can measure memorization as much as retrieval | | Meta-evaluation | **Weak** | No tests reference `evals/`; CI does not run it; no adversarial fixtures or human audit | The scorer's failure modes are unknown until someone probes them | | Process adherence | **Weak** | Rule requires before/after runs for prompt/tool/Pi changes; 110 commits touched those paths since 2026-09-24; 0 commits touched `evals/`; no eval result after that date | A voluntary gate that is not run is not a gate | | Cost and latency | **Adequate** | Wall time and tokens measured; all 22 rows have `cost_usd = 0` because no `cost` block is configured | Token counts are useful; dollar cost is unmeasured | | Privacy and ethics | **Strong** | Isolated homes; telemetry off; keys env-only; content-free telemetry in the product | Research artifacts can be sensitive; this is handled well | | Documentation honesty | **Strong** | README caveats, known issues, refusal disclosures, explicit "single run is noisy" | Readers are warned about the main limitations | **Overall:** the infrastructure is solid; the measurement is narrower than the claims; the operating discipline has decayed. A fair one-line summary is: *good smoke test, not yet a benchmark.* --- ## 4. Meta-eval: can the scorer be fooled? I wrote eight synthetic artifacts for `q01` ("test-time compute scaling for LLM reasoning") and ran the repo's own scorer with `--rescore`. This tests the measurement instrument, not the model. The fixtures, command, and raw output are in `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/`. Command: ```sh git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Companion-Inc/feynman.git /tmp/feynman-src python3 experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_fixtures.py cd /tmp/feynman-src node evals/run.mjs --rescore /work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/fixtures.jsonl ``` ### Results | Case | Artifact content | `done` | `valid` | `title` | `recall` | Reading | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | f1-control | Correct claim + correct paper, URL, exact title | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | All four surface metrics pass with no workflow | | f2-fake-id | Exact title, fabricated ID `2408.99999` | yes | 0% | – | 100% | `recall` is title string presence, not resolvability | | f3-irrelevant | Real paper, exact title, unrelated topic | yes | 100% | 100% | 0% | `valid`/`title` do not measure relevance | | f4-absurd-number | "Improves MATH accuracy by 1000%" + correct citation | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | No numeric or claim-support check | | f5-wrong-title | Correct ID, wrong bracketed title, claim text repeats title words | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | Title heuristic satisfied by surrounding prose (8/11 title tokens, 72.7%) | | f6-no-provenance | Correct artifact, no sidecar | no | – | – | 0% | `done` is filename existence; process gate works | | f7-bare-id | Exact title + bare `2408.03314` (no URL/prefix) | yes | – | – | 100% | ID extraction misses bare IDs; recall still sees them | | f8-rejected | Key paper only in a "Rejected sources" list | yes | 100% | 100% | 100% | Recall credits presence, not use | Raw scores: `experiments/feynman-eval-audit/fixtures.jsonl`, `fixtures.md`, `rescore.log`. ### What the probe establishes 1. **A synthetic one-paragraph artifact scores 100%.** `f1-control` has one sentence and a minimal provenance file. It passes `done`, `valid`, `title`, and `recall`. The scorer cannot distinguish it from a six-stage `/lit` run. This is expected from an outcome-based eval, but it means a perfect score is compatible with no research process at all. 2. **The title check has a false-positive mode.** `f5-wrong-title` attaches the title "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" to the correct ID for the test-time-compute paper. The line also contains the claim "test-time compute can be scaled more effectively than model parameters." Because the scorer compares the resolved title to the whole line, 8 of 11 title tokens overlap (72.7% ≥ 60%), so `title` passes. The README warns about short-name citations missing; it does not warn about prose satisfying the check. 3. **Recall is presence, not use.** `f2-fake-id` gets 100% recall with a fabricated ID because the exact title is present. `f8-rejected` gets 100% recall because the paper appears in a rejected-sources list. A report could "recall" every key paper while excluding it from the synthesis. 4. **There is no claim-level check.** `f4-absurd-number` claims a 1000% accuracy improvement and cites the correct paper. All four metrics pass. Identifier resolution and title overlap say nothing about whether the cited paper supports the sentence. 5. **`done` is a process gate only.** `f6-no-provenance` fails because the sidecar is missing; `f1-control` passes with a minimal sidecar that contains no real provenance. The metric checks existence, not content. 6. **Extraction is format-sensitive.** `f7-bare-id` is invisible to `cites` (0), but visible to `recall` (100%) because `keyRecall` does a raw substring match on the text. The same paper is simultaneously uncounted and counted. These are not exotic adversarial cases. Wrong-but-resolvable citations, rejected sources, bare IDs, and unsupported numbers are ordinary failure modes in research writing. The eval's own README is honest that it measures citation resolution rather than truth; the risk is that the summary table and release prose invite a stronger reading. --- ## 5. Release-claim audit The most specific public claim is in `RELEASES.md` for v0.5.3 (2026-09-24): > "On the `/lit` eval with GPT-5.6 Terra, 4 of 4 questions finished, all 44 citations resolved with matching titles, and each question ran the researcher, verifier, and reviewer in under 11 minutes (0.5.2: 9-14 minutes, 43 of 43 citations)." | Claim | Check | Result | Status | |---|---|---|---| | 4 of 4 questions finished | Read the 0.5.3 Terra JSONL | 4/4 `completed: true` | Recomputed, consistent | | 44 citations | Sum `citations` across q01/q04/q07/q10 | 11 + 11 + 7 + 15 = 44 distinct identifiers | Recomputed, consistent | | All 44 resolved | `citations_checked` = 44; all `citation_validity` = 1 | 44/44 | Recomputed, consistent | | Matching titles | All `title_match` = 1 | 44/44 by the 60% heuristic | Recomputed, but heuristic-dependent | | Under 11 minutes each | `wall_s` = 652, 628, 578, 650 | Max 652 s = 10.87 min | Recomputed, consistent | | 0.5.2 baseline: 9–14 min, 43/43 | Find the 43-citation run | Only `2026-09-24-lit-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.jsonl` has 43 citations; it is labeled `feynman_version: 0.5.0` | **Metadata mismatch / unverified label** | | "44 citations" means 44 claims | Read `extractIds` | Map dedupes by ID; 44 distinct IDs, not 44 inline citation instances | Clarified; release wording is broader than the metric | | 0.5.3 runs are reproducible from a SHA | Read `git_dirty` | All four 0.5.3 rows have `git_dirty: true`; 14/22 rows overall are dirty | **Not reproducible from the recorded SHA alone** | | Cost | Read `usage.cost_usd` | All 22 rows are `$0`; no `cost` block in the example `models.json` | **Unmeasured** | | Search benchmark: 7/9 vs 2/9 seminal papers | Look for the benchmark in the repo | No benchmark file or result artifact; only the release note | **Unverified** | Two further facts matter for reading the claim: - **The eval is not currently a gate.** Since the last eval commit (`e2bcb84`, 2026-09-24), there have been 110 commits touching `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `extensions/`, or `package.json`; 47 of those touch prompts/agents/skills/extensions alone. `git log --since=2026-09-25 -- evals` returns 0 commits. No eval result after 2026-09-24 exists in the repo. Either the eval was not run, or it was run and not committed; both violate the README's rule. - **A concrete missed regression.** Commit `278e9af` (2026-11-05) changed `prompts/lit.md` because a live run improvised `parallel()` and its first workflow call failed. The fix was covered by a prompt-example unit test, not by the research eval. That is exactly the kind of failure the eval's `done` metric is designed to catch, and no post-fix eval result exists. ### What the 0.5.3 numbers do establish They establish that, on one GPT-5.6 Terra run over four questions, in a dirty worktree, four `/lit` artifacts were produced with a provenance file, and every extracted identifier in those four artifacts resolved and had ≥60% title-token overlap on a line. That is a real citation-hygiene result. It is not evidence of claim-level accuracy, synthesis quality, or generalization to the other eight questions, other workflows, or other models. ### Statistical context Treating the 44 identifiers as independent (optimistic, because they cluster within four reports), a 95% Wilson interval for 44/44 is roughly [0.92, 1.00]. Treating the four questions as the unit, 4/4 completion has a Wilson interval of roughly [0.51, 1.00]. The true uncertainty is wider than either because there is one run per condition and no repeated sampling. "100%" in the table is a point estimate, not a ceiling. --- [123 more lines in file. ## 6. Dogfooding notes

I ran this audit from inside a Feynman session and also exercised the installed CLI as a subprocess.

**Live one-shot probe.** In an empty workspace:

```sh
FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=off feynman --no-session --prompt \
  "Create the file outputs/probe-artifact.md with exactly one line: FEYNMAN_PROBE_OK. Use the write tool, then reply DONE."
```

Result: exit 0, stdout `DONE`, artifact `FEYNMAN_PROBE_OK` (17 bytes), and the harness created `outputs/`, `outputs/.plans/`, `outputs/.drafts/`, `notes/`, and `papers/`. Log: `experiments/feynman-harness-probe/probe.log`; result summary: `probe-result.txt`. This is a small positive data point: the one-shot path exits, writes the requested artifact, and scaffolds the expected workspace.

**What helped the audit.**

- The system prompt's evidence/integrity rules are unusually explicit: separate observation from inference, label blocked/unverified work, verify artifacts on disk, never invent results. Those rules directly shaped this report.
- Shell access plus a source-first workflow made it possible to audit the evaluator's code, not just its marketing. Many agent products make this impossible because only a hosted API is exposed.
- The harness's own conventions (slugged artifacts, provenance sidecars, raw logs) are good habits for any eval.

**Frictions observed.**

- **The eval is not shipped.** `evals/` and `tests/` are absent from the npm package (`package.json` `files`; README line 5). An installed user cannot run the harness's own eval without cloning the repo. That is a transparency cost.
- **There is no `feynman eval` command.** Running the eval means building the repo, supplying a `models.json`, exporting a provider key, and choosing ids/workflow manually. That is developer-only, which helps explain why the rule decays.
- **`--rescore` depends on author-local state.** Every committed row stores an absolute `workdir` (`/Users/advaitpaliwal/.cache/...` or `/var/folders/...`). The artifacts are not committed. A fresh clone cannot rescore any published result.
- **Version and model skew.** The installed harness is 0.5.65; the source snapshot is 0.5.69. The committed evals use GPT-5.6 Terra / Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Sonnet 5; this session runs DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. I can audit the scorer and the claims, but not reproduce the model behavior.
- **The summary row hides denominators.** `table()` takes the unweighted mean of per-question percentages, excluding nulls (`run.mjs:251-259`). A run with 3/4 completion can show `valid 100%` because the failed question is null and dropped, while `recall` includes the failure as 0. The columns have different denominators. That is visible if you read carefully, but the "all" row encourages a single number.
- **Self-evaluation bias.** I am the harness. There is no independent human rater in this loop. The quantitative claims here trace to files and commands; the ratings are judgments and should be treated as such.

---

## 7. What would make this eval good

Prioritized, with acceptance criteria. The first three are cheap relative to another four-question model run.

### P0 — make the scorer trustworthy and the results reproducible

1. **Extract the scorer into an importable module and add `tests/eval-scorer.test.ts` with adversarial fixtures.** Encode the eight cases above. Assert current behavior explicitly, including known false positives, so a future scorer change cannot silently change their meaning. Add a `claim_support` column and make `f4-absurd-number` fail it.
   - *Acceptance:* `npm test` runs the scorer tests; CI fails if `f2` validity is not 0, `f3` recall is not 0, `f6` done is not false, or `f4` passes a claim-support check.
2. **Persist enough artifacts to rescore from a clone.** Commit a small tarball per run (final `.md`, provenance, extracted citation list) or make `workdir` a content-addressed relative path and publish the bundle. Do not commit 100 MB session logs by default; commit the scored artifact and a manifest.
   - *Acceptance:* `node evals/run.mjs --rescore evals/results/<file>.jsonl` works in a fresh clone with no author-local paths.
3. **Separate process compliance from output quality.** Replace the single `done` with `artifact_present`, `provenance_present`, `verifier_ran`, `reviewer_ran`, and `quality_metrics`. Derive the stage flags from the session JSONL (subagent roles/calls), not filenames.
   - *Acceptance:* a run that skips the verifier/reviewer cannot score the same as one that runs them.

### P1 — make the measurement valid and powered

4. **Add a claim-level audit sample.** For each run, sample 20 numeric or causal claims and check whether the cited source contains the number/claim. Report claim precision with a denominator and a human-readable list of failures. This is the only way to catch the `f4` class.
   - *Acceptance:* a run with a fabricated 1000% number has a non-zero failure list.
5. **Run repeats and report uncertainty.** Two or three seeds per condition, or at least two independent runs for a prompt change. Report mean/range and n. Use all 12 questions when the budget allows; otherwise state the selected ids as a fixed panel and do not generalize.
   - *Acceptance:* no "100%" claim appears without n and an interval or range.
6. **Enforce the rule or narrow it.** If the rule stays, add a PR checklist/CI check: changes to `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `extensions/`, or the Pi pin must include a new eval result file or a written `no-eval` justification. If full evals are too expensive for every change, define a cheap gate (one question, scorer tests) plus a release gate (four questions, two seeds).
   - *Acceptance:* the repository can show, for each prompt change, either a result file or an explicit waiver. Today it can show neither.
7. **Add contamination controls.** Include 3–5 post-cutoff questions; run a no-tools baseline; and run a "titles only" control to estimate how much recall comes from memorization. Keep the canonical questions for comparability, but do not treat them as retrieval evidence by themselves.

### P2 — extend coverage and accounting

8. **Measure cost.** Add a `cost` block to the example `models.json`; report dollars per completed question and per valid citation. The current `$0.00` is a missing value, not a cheap run.
9. **Cover the other workflows.** `/deepresearch` is already supported by the runner but has no committed result. Add at least one `/audit` case with a known paper–code discrepancy (the README already names SciCoQA's 92 discrepancies) and one `/review` case with a known flawed draft.
10. **Meta-metrics.** Report citation precision/recall against a human-labeled sample, inter-rater agreement for any human judgments, and the false-positive rate of the verifier. A benchmark of the benchmark.

---

## 8. General lessons for AI-eval quality

1. **Deterministic scorers buy reproducibility at the cost of construct validity.** That is a reasonable trade for a smoke test. The mistake is letting the metric's name do more work than its implementation.
2. **Meta-evaluate the scorer before trusting the score.** Eight hand-written fixtures found four false-positive modes; scoring them took seconds. A scorer without adversarial fixtures is an untested measuring instrument.
3. **A rule that is not in CI decays.** The eval README's rule is well written and was followed during the initial Sept 23–24 burst. Then 110 eval-relevant commits passed without an eval commit. Voluntary gates lose to release pressure.
4. **`done` is a process metric, not a quality metric.** Filename existence and provenance presence are useful checks; they are not evidence of research quality. Report them separately.
5. **Canonical-paper recall tests memory as much as retrieval.** Test-time compute, speculative decoding, CRISPR base editing, and mixture-of-experts are well-known topics. Add post-cutoff and no-tool controls before interpreting recall as search skill.
6. **Report n, repeats, failures, and denominators.** A 4/4 result is a point estimate with a wide interval, not a 100% capability claim. Columns with different denominators should not share an "all" row without a note.
7. **Store raw artifacts.** A JSONL row with an absolute local `workdir` is a receipt, not a reproduction. If the artifact is gone, the score is not independently checkable.
8. **Citation validity is not claim support.** A resolving DOI and a matching title are necessary but far from sufficient. The research-quality question is whether the source supports the sentence, and that needs a claim-level check.

These lessons generalize beyond Feynman: they apply to any agent harness that reports citation precision, "verified" labels, or benchmark scores from a handful of runs.

---

## 9. Open questions

- Was the eval run outside the repository after 2026-09-24? If so, where are the results, and why were they not committed as the README requires?
- Why only q01, q04, q07, and q10? Budget, runtime, or model refusals? The committed results cannot tell.

- How do human experts score the same four artifacts? What is the correlation between `valid`/`title`/`recall` and expert judgments of claim support?

content.text:
# Adversarial review: `outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md`

**Reviewer role:** evidence-integrity audit (skeptical, adversarial)
**Target:** `/work/outputs/feynman-harness-eval-quality.md`
**Pinned source:** `/tmp/feynman-src` @ `11744290758648c2ecd7c0d6389cdca9ae580290` (HEAD `1174429`, package 0.5.69, 2026-11-13)
**Audit artifacts:** `/work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/`, `/work/experiments/feynman-harness-probe/`
**Verdict on the report itself:** no fatal errors found. The report's central claims reproduce. Two major overclaims/missing caveats and eight minor issues follow.

---

## Findings

### F1 — MAJOR — "110 commits" is presented as substantive churn, but 63/110 touch only `package.json` among the cited paths
**Location:** Bottom line ¶4 ("In that window, 110 commits touched those surfaces…"); §5 "Two further facts"; §8 lesson 3; §3 "Process adherence".
**Problem:** The literal count reproduces (`git log --since=2026-09-24 -- prompts .feynman/agents .feynman/SYSTEM.md skills extensions package.json` → 110; `git-stats.txt` records `eval_relevant_commits_since_2026-09-24: 110`). But the report never decomposes it, so a reader infers ~110 substantive prompt/tool changes. In fact:
- 63 of the 110 touch **only `package.json`** among the six rule paths;
- 51 of those 63 carry release/version-update subjects (e.g. `f39aec3 "Update pi-subagents to 0.88.1; release 0.5.69"`, `32cfff4 "Release 0.5.4"`);
- 1 of the 110 is a merge commit (109 non-merge), so the count double-counts at least one PR;
- the substantive prompt/agent/skill/extension/`SYSTEM.md` count is **47** (46 if `SYSTEM.md` is excluded).
The audit's own `git-stats.txt` records a much narrower `prompt_commits_since_2026-09-24: 6`, which the report does not mention. The verdict ("decayed operating discipline") still holds on 47 substantive changes, but "110" overstates the evidence roughly 2.3×.
**Evidence:** `git log` decomposition (see above); `/work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/git-stats.txt:11-12`.

### F2 — MINOR — "47 of those touch prompts/agents/skills/extensions alone" is off by one
**Location:** §5 "Two further facts", first bullet.
**Problem:** 46 commits touch `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `skills/`, `extensions/`. The 47th is a commit that also/instead touches `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, which the same sentence lists separately ("…or `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`…"). Either say "47 including `SYSTEM.md`" or "46 excluding it".
**Evidence:** `git log --since=2026-09-24 --oneline -- prompts .feynman/agents skills extensions | wc -l` → 46; adding `.feynman/SYSTEM.md` → 47. `git-stats.txt` contains no 47; its only prompt count is 6.

### F3 — MAJOR — "Determinism: Strong" omits that scoring depends on live arXiv/Crossref responses, and that a committed row was manually re-scored after a lookup failure
**Location:** §2 "What is genuinely good" ("**Determinism.** … The same artifact text and the same live metadata produce the same score."); §2 metric table `valid` row; §3 scorecard row "Isolation and determinism | **Strong** | … | Removes the largest sources of accidental variance".
**Problem:** `valid` is not a property of the artifact alone. `scoreCitations` computes `checked = rows.filter(r => r.resolves !== undefined)` (`evals/run.mjs:183`), so a network/API failure silently **removes** an identifier from both the `valid` numerator and denominator and never lists it in `unresolved`. `evals/README.md:48` says this explicitly ("Lookups that fail on the network are left out"). More importantly, two committed result summaries state: **"q01 citation validity was re-scored after a transient lookup failure."** That is a manual re-score, not a deterministic single pass, and it is in the very files the report says it read ("all committed result files", §1). A transient failure can therefore yield `valid: 100%` on a shrunken denominator, which is exactly the reading the report warns against elsewhere. The "Strong" rating and "same score" sentence need this caveat; at minimum the report should note `citations` vs `citations_checked` as the audit check.
**Evidence:** `evals/README.md:48`; `evals/run.mjs:183,188`; `evals/results/2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.md:3`; `…-claude-opus-5-5.md:3`.

### F4 — MINOR — the f7 fixture is confounded: the exact title alone guarantees `recall`, so it does not show that recall "sees" a bare ID
**Location:** §4 table `f7-bare-id`; §4 "What the probe establishes" item 6 ("visible to `recall` (100%) because `keyRecall` does a raw substring match on the text").
**Problem:** `f7` contains **both** the exact key-paper title and the bare ID. `keyRecall` (`evals/run.mjs:198`) passes on `normed.includes(norm(p.title))` regardless of the ID, so `recall = 100%` is guaranteed by the title. The fixture cannot isolate the claimed bare-ID behavior; a bare ID with a *non-exact* title would be needed. The broader conclusion ("recall is presence, not use") is still true and is independently visible in the code, but this specific inference is unsupported by the fixture.
**Evidence:** `/work/experiments/feynman-eval-audit/make_fixtures.py` (`f7-bare-id` body); `evals/run.mjs:198`.

### F5 — MINOR — "4 questions per run" is false for one of the six committed runs
**Location:** §3 scorecard "Statistical power | Weak | 4 questions per run…".
**Problem:** `2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-ferrylane_claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` has **2** rows (q01, q10). Its `.md` explains why: "Only the non-biology questions were run: Opus 5.5 refuses q04 and q07." "Typical run is four questions" is fine; the blanket "4 questions per run" is not.
**Evidence:** `evals/results/2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-ferrylane_claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` (2 lines); `…-claude-opus-5-5.md:3`.

### F6 — MINOR — §9 open question "the committed results cannot tell" is partly answered by the committed results
**Location:** §9, "Why only q01, q04, q07, and q10? Budget, runtime, or model refusals? The committed results cannot tell."
**Problem:** The Opus subset **is** explained in the committed `.md` ("Only the non-biology questions were run: Opus 5.5 refuses q04 and q07"), and `RELEASES.md` documents the same refusal as a known issue. What remains genuinely unexplained is why *Terra* used the same four-id panel. The sentence overstates the unavailability of the answer.
**Evidence:** `evals/results/2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-ferrylane_claude-opus-5-5.md:3`; `RELEASES.md:484`; `evals/results/2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-ferrylane_claude-opus-5-5.jsonl` (q04 exit 1, q07 exit 1).

### F7 — MINOR — live-probe reproduction command in the report does not match the recorded command
**Location:** §6 "Live one-shot probe" code block; §1 table "Live probe".
**Problem:** The report's command sets `FEYNMAN_TELEMETRY=off feynman --no-session --prompt …`. The recorded command line in `probe-result.txt` is `feynman --no-session --prompt '…'` with no env assignment. The outcome (exit 0, `DONE`, 17 bytes, `.plans/`/`.drafts/`/`notes/`/`papers/`) does reproduce from the artifacts, but the exact command shown is not the one recorded.
**Evidence:** `/work/experiments/feynman-harness-probe/probe-result.txt` (`command:` line); `…/outputs/probe-artifact.md` (17 bytes, `FEYNMAN_PROBE_OK\n`).

### F8 — MINOR — `README line 5` is cited for the absence of `tests/` too, but line 5 only covers `evals/`
**Location:** §6 "The eval is not shipped. `evals/` and `tests/` are absent from the npm package (`package.json` `files`; README line 5)."
**Problem:** `evals/README.md:5` says only "This directory is not in the npm package". The absence of `tests/` is true (verified against `package.json.files`) but is not supported by the cited README line. This is the same "citation attached to a claim that does not support the exact wording" failure the report itself audits.
**Evidence:** `evals/README.md:5`; `package.json.files` (neither `evals/` nor `tests/` listed).

### F9 — MINOR — "exactly the kind of failure the eval's `done` metric is designed to catch" overstates `done`
**Location:** §5 "A concrete missed regression" (commit `278e9af`).
**Problem:** `278e9af` fixes a prompt after "a live run improvised `parallel()` and its first workflow call failed." `done` checks only that a largest `outputs/*.md` and its `.provenance.md` exist (`evals/run.mjs:87-94`). A run can have a failed first workflow call and still recover to produce both files. The failure mode `done` demonstrably catches is the *pre-wait* `bg_wait` case (Terra q04, `completed: false`), not an arbitrary failed tool call.
**Evidence:** `git show -s 278e9af`; `evals/run.mjs:87-94`; `evals/results/2026-09-24-lit-0.5.3-pre-wait-ferrylane-openai_gpt-5.6-terra.md:3`.

### F10 — MINOR — "eight fixtures found four false-positive modes" is oversold; three are restatements of the documented metric definitions
**Location:** §8 lesson 2.
**Problem:** `f3` (relevance), `f4` (numeric claims), and `f8` (rejected-source presence) follow directly from what `evals/README.md` already says each metric measures (`valid` = resolves; `recall` = "appear in the final output"). Only `f5` (prose satisfying the title-overlap check) is a genuinely undocumented false-positive mode, plus `f7`'s extraction inconsistency. Presenting all four as discoveries inflates the meta-eval's contribution.
**Evidence:** `evals/README.md:48-50`; §4 results table.

---

## Category coverage (explicit no-issue statements)

11:But the eval is a **citation-hygiene smoke test, not a research-quality benchmark**. Committed results cover only four of its twelve questions, only `/lit` has results, and the typical run is one pass over four questions with no repeats or uncertainty estimates. Its four headline metrics measure filename existence (`done`), identifier resolvability (`valid`), a 60% title-token overlap heuristic (`title`), and string presence of one or two expected papers (`recall`). None measures whether a cited source supports the claim attached to it.
15:No committed eval result exists after 2026-09-24, even though the eval's own rule says to run it before and after any prompt, tool, extension, or Pi-version change. In that window, 110 commits touched those surfaces, including a November 5 fix to the `/lit` prompt after a live workflow failure, and **zero commits touched `evals/`**. The rule is well written but not operationalized in CI.
93:- **Determinism.** The scorer is a readable ~300-line Node script with no LLM judge. The same artifact text and the same live metadata produce the same score.
114:| Statistical power | **Weak** | 4 questions per run, one run per condition, no repeats or intervals; 4/4 completion has a 95% Wilson interval of roughly [0.51, 1.0] | 100% on n=4 is not a 100% capability claim |
118:| Process adherence | **Weak** | Rule requires before/after runs for prompt/tool/Pi changes; 110 commits touched those paths since 2026-09-24; 0 commits touched `evals/`; no eval result after that date | A voluntary gate that is not run is not a gate |
150:| f7-bare-id | Exact title + bare `2408.03314` (no URL/prefix) | yes | – | – | 100% | ID extraction misses bare IDs; recall still sees them |
162:6. **Extraction is format-sensitive.** `f7-bare-id` is invisible to `cites` (0), but visible to `recall` (100%) because `keyRecall` does a raw substring match on the text. The same paper is simultaneously uncounted and counted.
189:- **The eval is not currently a gate.** Since the last eval commit (`e2bcb84`, 2026-09-24), there have been 110 commits touching `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `extensions/`, or `package.json`; 47 of those touch prompts/agents/skills/extensions alone. `git log --since=2026-09-25 -- evals` returns 0 commits. No eval result after 2026-09-24 exists in the repo. Either the eval was not run, or it was run and not committed; both violate the README's rule.
190:- **A concrete missed regression.** Commit `278e9af` (2026-11-05) changed `prompts/lit.md` because a live run improvised `parallel()` and its first workflow call failed. The fix was covered by a prompt-example unit test, not by the research eval. That is exactly the kind of failure the eval's `done` metric is designed to catch, and no post-fix eval result exists.
194:They establish that, on one GPT-5.6 Terra run over four questions, in a dirty worktree, four `/lit` artifacts were produced with a provenance file, every extracted identifier in those four artifacts resolved, and every row's `title_match` was 1 under the 60% heuristic. That is a real citation-hygiene result. It is not evidence of claim-level accuracy, synthesis quality, or generalization to the other eight questions, other workflows, or other models.
198:Treating the 44 identifiers as independent (optimistic, because they cluster within four reports), a 95% Wilson interval for 44/44 is roughly [0.92, 1.00]. Treating the four questions as the unit, 4/4 completion has a Wilson interval of roughly [0.51, 1.00]. The true uncertainty is wider than either because there is one run per condition and no repeated sampling. "100%" in the table is a point estimate, not a ceiling.
251:6. **Enforce the rule or narrow it.** If the rule stays, add a PR checklist/CI check: changes to `prompts/`, `.feynman/agents/`, `.feynman/SYSTEM.md`, `skills/`, `extensions/`, or the Pi pin must include a new eval result file or a written `no-eval` justification. If full evals are too expensive for every change, define a cheap gate (one question, scorer tests) plus a release gate (four questions, two seeds).
266:2. **Meta-evaluate the scorer before trusting the score.** Eight hand-written fixtures found four false-positive modes; scoring them took seconds. A scorer without adversarial fixtures is an untested measuring instrument.
